content: Sickle cell disease is a genetic disorder affecting hemoglobin, which leads to the production of abnormally shaped red blood cells. These cells are rigid and can obstruct blood vessels, causing acute painful episodes and other complications. Recent therapeutic approaches have aimed to rehydrate these sickled cells by reducing water and ion loss, but the efficacy and safety of such treatments remain unclear. This document represents an updated review of previously published findings. The objective of this review was to evaluate the risks and benefits of drugs designed to rehydrate sickled red blood cells. To achieve this, researchers conducted a comprehensive search of the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis and Genetic Disorders Group's Haemoglobinopathies Trials Register and online trial registries for ongoing studies as of July 1, 2018. The last search of the Haemoglobinopathies Trials Register was conducted on October 8, 2018. The inclusion criteria were randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials comparing these drugs to either placebo or alternative treatments. Out of 51 studies identified, only three met the inclusion criteria, involving a total of 524 participants aged 12 to 65 years with sickle cell disease. One study evaluated the effects of zinc sulfate compared to placebo, while the other two investigated senicapoc, a Gardos channel blocker, against placebo. In the zinc sulfate study, which included 145 participants, there was a significant reduction in the frequency of painful crises over a period of 1.5 years. The mean difference was -2.83 (95% confidence interval: -3.51 to -2.15), based on moderate-quality evidence. However, the analysis was limited by insufficient statistical data. Changes in red blood cell parameters and blood counts were inconsistent, and the evidence for these outcomes was of very low quality. Importantly, no serious adverse events were reported in this study. The Phase II dose-finding study of senicapoc demonstrated that high-dose senicapoc significantly improved hemoglobin levels, reduced the number and proportion of dense red blood cells, and improved red blood cell indices and hematocrit values. However, the evidence supporting these findings was of very low quality. Low-dose senicapoc produced similar but less pronounced effects. Despite these improvements in red blood cell parameters, there was no difference in the frequency of painful crises between the high-dose, low-dose, and placebo groups, based on low-quality evidence. A subsequent Phase III trial of senicapoc was terminated prematurely because no difference was observed between the treatment and control groups in the primary endpoint, which was the frequency of painful crises. The authors concluded that while zinc sulfate shows promise in reducing sickle cell-related crises, larger, multicenter, long-term studies are necessary to confirm its effectiveness. Although senicapoc improved red blood cell survival in a dose-dependent manner, this did not translate into a reduction in painful crises. Given that research in this area is no longer active, the review will not be updated further.
